extract:
R.E.M. formed in Athens, Georgia, in 1980, emerging from the college-town party and club scene that also produced the B-52's and Pylon. The band was active until 2011, when they announced an amicable split after more than three decades together. Their sound, built on Peter Buck's chiming arpeggiated guitar, Mike Mills's melodic bass and harmony vocals, Bill Berry's economical drumming, and Michael Stipe's oblique, often mumbled lyrics, became a template for American alternative rock.

The four met as students around the University of Georgia. Buck was working at Wuxtry Records when Stipe, a regular customer, struck up a friendship with him over shared tastes in punk and art rock, including Patti Smith, Television, and the Velvet Underground. Berry and Mills, who had played together in high school bands in Macon, joined soon after. Their first show was at a birthday party held in a converted church. In 1981 they recorded the single Radio Free Europe for the small Hib-Tone label, produced by Mitch Easter. Its success on college radio led to a deal with I.R.S. Records and the 1982 EP Chronic Town.

Their debut album Murmur (1983), produced by Easter and Don Dixon, was named album of the year by Rolling Stone, beating Michael Jackson's Thriller. Reckoning (1984) followed with the same producers and included So. Central Rain. For Fables of the Reconstruction (1985), the band recorded in London with Joe Boyd. The result was a murkier, Southern Gothic record that included Driver 8. Lifes Rich Pageant (1986), produced by Don Gehman, sharpened Stipe's vocals and politics on songs like Fall on Me and Cuyahoga. Document (1987), co-produced with Scott Litt, gave them their first Top 10 hit, The One I Love, along with the breathless It's the End of the World as We Know It (And I Feel Fine).

In 1988 R.E.M. left I.R.S. for Warner Bros. and released Green, which carried Stand, Orange Crush, and World Leader Pretend. Out of Time (1991), featuring Losing My Religion and a guest appearance by KRS-One on Radio Song, made them global stars and won multiple Grammys. Automatic for the People (1992), with John Paul Jones contributing string arrangements, produced Everybody Hurts and Man on the Moon. They followed it with the distorted rock of Monster (1994) and New Adventures in Hi-Fi (1996). Berry left in 1997 after suffering a brain aneurysm on tour two years earlier. As a trio the band made Up, Reveal, and Around the Sun before returning to a rawer sound with Accelerate (2008) and Collapse into Now (2011).

Alongside contemporaries such as the Replacements, Hüsker Dü, and the Minutemen, R.E.M. proved that a band nurtured on college radio and independent labels could reach the mainstream without abandoning its identity. Bands including Nirvana, Pavement, and Radiohead acknowledged their influence. R.E.M. was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2007 and the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2024, where the four original members briefly performed together. Since the breakup the members have pursued separate projects, and they have repeatedly said there will be no reunion. Meanwhile, anniversary reissues of their I.R.S. and Warner catalogs have kept the music in circulation.
title: R.E.M.
